The upload comes before the switch because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to request. Once every new file is in place, changing the manifest makes the new release live in a single step.

That includes users mid-session who lazy-load a script or stylesheet later. If those files were deleted, those users would hit missing files until they reloaded. Every release has two steps, and their order matters.

First, we upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images, fonts) under a versioned name, usually a content hash such as `app.3f9a1c.js`. Nothing references these files yet, so uploading them has no effect on live traffic.

Second, we switch the manifest, the HTML or JSON that tells browsers which asset names to load, to the new names. That switch is the actual release.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch makes the release live immediately. If it went out before the assets, any browser that fetched the new manifest would request files that don't exist yet and get 404s, which means broken pages, missing styles and failed script loads until the upload caught up. Uploading first guarantees that every name the new manifest references already exists when the first browser asks for it. Because the switch is a single small change, the release is effectively atomic: each browser sees either the complete old version or the complete new version, never a mix.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still holds the old asset names. It may be partway through a page load, lazy-loading a route chunk minutes later, or running from a cached HTML page or a long-lived tab. If we deleted the old files on release, those browsers would hit 404s for code they legitimately expect, and users would see breakage they did nothing to cause. Keeping the old versions lets every client finish with the version it started on. Versioned names also mean old and new files never collide, so both sets can be served side by side, and the old files can be cached indefinitely because their contents never change under a given name.

Rollback follows the same logic: point the manifest back at the previous names, which are still there.

Old assets can be removed once no reasonable client could still reference them, after the longest realistic tab lifetime or cache TTL has passed, not at release time.

A release has two steps. First, upload every new asset (scripts, stylesheets, images) under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, so it never overwrites an existing file. Second, switch the manifest so it references those new names. The manifest is the only file that changes in place, and that single update is what publishes the release.

The upload comes before the switch so the manifest never points at a file that isn't there yet. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the upload finished would request assets that return 404s, and the page would load broken or partly styled. With the uploads already complete, every name in the new manifest resolves the moment the manifest goes live, so the release takes effect all at once.

We keep the old assets because browsers that already loaded the previous manifest keep requesting the files it names. That covers open tabs fetching code-split chunks later, pages served from cache, and users partway through loading when the switch happens. If we deleted those files, those sessions would break even though they did nothing wrong. Keeping them lets each browser finish with the release it started on and pick up the new one on its next manifest fetch. It also makes rollback simple: switching the manifest back works immediately because the old files are still there.

Our releases happen in two steps: we upload the new assets, then we switch the manifest to point at them. Keeping that order, and leaving old assets in place, means no visitor ever loads a page that references a file that isn't there.

**How a release works**

1. Every built asset (JS bundles, CSS, images, fonts) gets a versioned name, usually a content hash such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. A changed file gets a new name, so it never overwrites the previous version.
2. We upload all of the new assets to the host or CDN. Nothing references them yet, so visitors don't see any change.
3. We switch the manifest, the entry point that maps logical names to versioned files (often `index.html` or a JSON manifest). From then on, new page loads get the new assets.
4. Old assets stay where they are. We don't delete them as part of the release.

**Why the upload comes before the switch**

Once the manifest switches, browsers immediately start requesting the files it names. If any of those files aren't uploaded yet, the requests return 404. The page then loads without its styles or scripts, or a lazy-loaded chunk fails partway through a session. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the first browser asks for it. The switch is a single small change, so the release is effectively atomic: visitors get either the full old version or the full new version, never a mix.

This order also makes failures safe. If the upload fails halfway, the live manifest still points at the old assets, and the extra new files just sit unused. We can retry the upload without affecting anyone.

**Why we keep the old assets**

A browser that loaded the page before the switch still holds the old manifest. It keeps requesting old asset names for as long as that page stays open. This happens when it lazy-loads a route chunk, fetches a font, or pulls an image further down the page. Cached HTML on the CDN or in the browser can also serve the old manifest for a while after the switch. If we deleted the old assets, all of those requests would 404, and users with open tabs would see broken pages or failed navigation in the middle of a session.

Keeping old assets also makes rollback cheap. Rolling back just means pointing the manifest at the previous version, because every file it needs is still there.

Because versioned names never collide, keeping old files costs only storage. Clean them up separately, well after a release, once no live manifest can still reference them. Deleting them during the deploy causes the failures described above.
